title: Oil Just Had Its Worst Week Since the War Began. India — the World's Third-Largest Importer — Hasn't Cut Fuel Prices by a Single Rupee.
excerpt: Brent crashed 11% to $72, Saudi Aramco restarted its biggest terminal, and an RBI official says $70 oil could push India back to 7% growth. But petrol and diesel remain ₹7.50 a litre above pre-war levels.
body:
The numbers tell a story the government would rather not discuss yet.

Brent crude settled at $71.99 a barrel on Friday, down 4.3% on the day and 10.9% for the week — its steepest weekly decline since the Iran war began on February 28. West Texas Intermediate finished at $69.23, crashing below $70 for the first time since before American and Israeli forces struck Iran four months ago. Both benchmarks have now erased virtually the entire geopolitical premium that once pushed oil above $120 a barrel at the height of the conflict.

"There is a growing sense that oil is going to keep moving through the Strait of Hormuz," said Phil Flynn, senior analyst at Price Futures Group. "We're going to get a flood of oil."

The Terminal That Signals the All-Clear

The clearest sign that the Gulf oil machine is grinding back to life came not from a diplomat but from a shipping terminal. Saudi Aramco resumed crude loadings on Friday at its Ras Tanura facility — the world's largest oil export terminal — after a nearly four-month halt. Two very large crude carriers, each capable of loading 2 million barrels, took on Saudi crude, with another waiting nearby, according to shipping data from LSEG.

Since March 8, Saudi exports had been rerouted to the Red Sea port of Yanbu via the East-West Pipeline after the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed. Now, Ras Tanura's restart suggests Riyadh believes conditions have stabilised enough to resume operations at its primary Gulf outlet.

Iraq is ramping up exports. Kuwait is restoring production. The UAE has even left OPEC. Iran is marketing crude across Asia. And Saudi Arabia — the world's largest exporter — may slash its August selling prices for Asian buyers by $6.50 to $8 per barrel from July levels, bringing them to a four-month low, according to a Reuters survey of four industry sources.

For India, the Maths Are Enormous

India imports more than 85% of the crude it consumes — roughly 5 million barrels a day. Before the war, about half came from the Middle East. Every $10 drop in the price of oil saves India an estimated $15 billion to $17 billion annually on its import bill and directly eases pressure on its current account deficit, fiscal balance, and inflation trajectory.

Nagesh Kumar, an external member of the Reserve Bank of India's monetary policy committee, told Bloomberg this week that oil prices around $70 a barrel could put India back on track for 7% economic growth or better in the fiscal year through March 2027. Just three weeks ago, the RBI had downgraded its growth projection to 6.6%, citing uncertainty over when the Middle East crisis would end.

The RBI's Governor, Sanjay Malhotra, has also calmed markets by telling ET Now that it is "premature to discuss rate hikes," noting that the central bank does not yet see inflation becoming broad-based. Lower-for-longer borrowing costs, combined with cheaper crude, could support corporate earnings, consumption, and equity valuations — Indian shares rallied on the news this week, with the Sensex gaining more than 1%.

The Price at the Pump Hasn't Moved

But here is where the relief ends for ordinary Indians. During the oil spike, the government raised petrol and diesel prices by ₹7.50 per litre each. Despite Brent falling from $120 to $72 — a 40% decline — retail fuel prices have not been cut by a single rupee.

State-owned oil marketing companies — Indian Oil Corporation, Bharat Petroleum, and Hindustan Petroleum — were estimated to be losing roughly ₹700 crore a day during the worst of the price surge. Those losses are now shrinking fast. The government also implemented a ₹10 per litre fuel tax cut in March to partially shield consumers, but it has not passed through the subsequent crude price crash.

"It is yet to be seen when the government will transfer the benefit of declining crude oil prices to retail consumers," The Bridge Chronicle reported on Friday.

Industry analysts suggest the financial benefits of cheaper crude will likely reflect only in the July-September earnings of refiners, since they are currently processing high-cost crude purchased months ago. Maintaining the current retail rate structure while input costs fall could yield windfall profits for the September quarter — profits the government may prefer to use to claw back its own pandemic-era and war-era deficits.

Indian Refiners Are Already Shopping Again

Behind the scenes, India's refineries are quietly rebuilding their Middle Eastern supply lines. Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia all curtailed supplies or failed to deliver contracted volumes during the Hormuz disruption. Those nations are once again ready to meet their commitments, and some Indian refiners have already begun placing orders and arranging logistics, according to Outlook Business.

Russia, meanwhile, has resumed offering discounts on crude — reversing the hefty premiums charged after the war began. India's Russian oil imports hit a record 2.66 million barrels per day in recent months, filling the gap left by the Gulf disruption. Now, with Middle Eastern supplies returning and prices collapsing, Indian buyers have leverage they haven't had in months.

Dubai cash premiums — a key pricing benchmark for Asian crude — fell into a discount of $1.64 a barrel this week, the lowest level in six years. The buyer's market that India's refiners have been waiting for appears to have arrived.

The Catch: This Isn't Over

For all the optimism, the ceasefire that enabled this oil-price collapse remains fragile. On Thursday, an Iranian drone struck a cargo ship near Oman's coast. Washington responded Friday with strikes on Iranian missile and drone storage sites. Tehran claims its navy struck back at U.S. positions.

The 60-day memorandum of understanding signed on June 17 between Washington and Tehran was supposed to reopen the strait and freeze hostilities while nuclear talks proceed. But with both sides accusing each other of violating its terms within days, analysts remain cautious.

"We are still living by the day," an unnamed industry source told The Economic Times.

For India, the stakes are unusually high. The country's entire economic trajectory — from GDP growth to the rupee's stability to the price of a litre of petrol — hinges on whether this oil crash holds, or whether the next drone strike sends prices spiralling back above $100.

For now, the tankers are loading. The prices are falling. And Indian consumers are still waiting for anyone to notice.
